thesis: This episode argues that TSMC's founder, Morris Chang, successfully pivoted the company from a troubled semiconductor model to a dominant foundry business by securing key customers like NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and Intel. The narrative highlights how TSMC became the world's only trillion-dollar company not on the US West Coast, solving financial problems and establishing itself as a critical global trade partner.

claims.claim: McKinsey identified Boeing as a functionalized company, but Ben notes it has commercial and government divisions and doesn't divide by fab like TSMC.
claims.quote: Then Don Brooks said, well, tell me one company, one big company that's functionalized, and McKinsey immediately answered Boeing, which is a good answer. Ben: Yeah, except it's not true. Boeing has commercial and government.

claims.claim: Morris Chang notes NVIDIA became a major customer of TSMC and one of the top five customers after the RIVA 128 chip success.
claims.quote: He told me that NVIDIA was in financial difficulties, but the chip that he wanted now to have foundried would not only save the company, it will also make NVIDIA a major customer of TSMC. That was actually quite a bold statement.

claims.claim: Chang confirms NVIDIA's prediction came true, solving financial problems and becoming one of the biggest five customers of TSMC.
claims.quote: In fact, his prediction came true. Not only did it solve ambiguous financial problems, it prevented from being bankrupt. Not only did it do that, it also started to make them a major customer of TSMC within two or three years. They did become one of the biggest five customers of TSMC.

claims.claim: Chang states that Apple came later as a customer of TSMC.
claims.quote: Apple, yeah. Apple came later. In my call with Jensen, he was still very friendly with me, but he also reminded me in a very serious tone that we had the quality delivery manufacturing problem on the 40-nanometer.

claims.claim: NVIDIA was a customer of TSMC and the dispute was resolved with a significant financial offer.
claims.quote: I called the salespeople that happened in direct contact with NVIDIA. Of course, I called everybody that was somewhat involved in the problem. It was a matter of money.

claims.claim: Qualcomm was another important customer besides NVIDIA and Intel.
claims.quote: David: Not just NVIDIA, but Qualcomm and Intel. Morris: Yeah, and it was a very important note.

claims.claim: Intel was another important customer besides NVIDIA and Qualcomm.
claims.quote: David: Not just NVIDIA, but Qualcomm and Intel. Morris: Yeah, and it was a very important note.

claims.claim: The previous CEO of TSMC's new businesses is now running MediaTek.
claims.quote: Ben: And he's now running MediaTek, is that correct? Morris: He's now the vice-chairman and the CEO of MediaTek, yeah.

claims.claim: Morris Chang had a lot of experience at Texas Instruments before TSMC.
claims.quote: Morris: Well, I know. Semiconductor industry people actually think the same way as I described. They all lay off people too. I had a lot of experience at Texas Instruments, but at Texas Instruments I was not a CEO.

claims.claim: IBM Semiconductor was in trouble because they were losing Qualcomm as a customer.
claims.quote: I immediately knew that IBM Semiconductor was in trouble. They had their own fabs and so on, but their main business was really supplying to Qualcomm and a few other very small fabless company. I immediately knew IBM was in trouble because they were losing Qualcomm.

claims.claim: The business Qualcomm gave TSMC increased rapidly after the 1997-1998 period.
claims.quote: Our business with Qualcomm, the business that Qualcomm gave us pretty rapidly increased after that 1997–1998 period.

claims.claim: UMC accepted IBM but later regretted their acceptance seriously a few years later.
claims.quote: So they immediately went to UMC. UMC accepted them only to regret seriously their acceptance a few years later.

claims.claim: TSMC was the only trillion-dollar company in the world not on the West Coast of the United States.
claims.quote: One question, David and I wanted to ask you is TSMC is essentially the only trillion-dollar company in the world not on the West Coast of the United States.
